claims.text: In high-entropy superconducting alloys, variations in the density of states at the Fermi level induced by electronic doping predominantly determine the superconducting transition temperature rather than atomic-scale disorder.
The proposed initial alloy is homogeneous, single-phase, and bcc.
(TaNb)1-x(HfZrTi)x behaves as a weak- to intermediate-coupling, isotropic single-band s-wave BCS superconductor.
Systematic compositional variation in (TaNb)1-x(HfZrTi)x changes its electron count through electronic doping.
Electronic doping caused by compositional variation changes the density of states at the Fermi level.
Keeping the processing route and cooling rate constant will keep overall atomic disorder nearly constant across compositions.
Changes in the density of states at the Fermi level alter the electron–phonon coupling strength.
Within a classical BCS framework, changes in the density of states at the Fermi level can change Tc.
When disorder is comparable between samples, differences in Tc favor an electronic-structure explanation over a disorder-driven explanation.
Higher electron doping will enhance the density of states at the Fermi level.
A composition with higher electron doping and enhanced density of states will have a higher Tc than the baseline at constant disorder.
Reducing the electron count will lower Tc.
The proposed mechanism is expected to apply while the alloy remains a stable, single-phase bcc material.
The proposed mechanism is restricted to the weak- to intermediate-electron–phonon-coupling regime.
Phase segregation or significant changes in disorder may cause deviations from the predicted density-of-states–Tc relationship.
The compared x = 0.35 and x = 0.71 films have comparable mean free paths of approximately 5–6 nm, indicating comparable microscopic disorder.
The reported Tc values differ between x = 0.35 and x = 0.71, with values of 6.7 ± 1.1 K and 4.3 ± 1.1 K, respectively.
A lack of systematic Tc changes despite significant measured density-of-states changes would falsify the hypothesis.
A stronger correlation of Tc with disorder indicators such as mean free path than with electronic doping would falsify the hypothesis.
